Rome. The capital of Italy and one of the oldest and most influential cities in human history. It remains the spiritual and administrative center of the Catholic Church and is dotted with monuments from millennia of history.

Rome was traditionally founded on April twenty-first in seven hundred fifty-three BCE. It grew from a settlement of Latin peoples on the Tiber River to dominate the Italian peninsula and eventually the Mediterranean world. The Roman Republic, lasting from roughly five hundred nine BCE to twenty-seven BCE, established representative government, law codes, and the Senate. These institutions influenced all later democracies and constitutional systems.

The Roman Empire was established by Augustus Caesar in twenty-seven BCE and expanded to rule from Britain to Mesopotamia. It lasted until four hundred seventy-six CE in the west, becoming the template for empire and governance. The Colosseum was built from seventy to eighty CE under the Flavian emperors and is the largest surviving Roman structure. It hosted gladiatorial combat and public spectacles and exemplifies Roman engineering and social spectacle.

Rome's legal traditions, codified in the Digest, Pandects, and Justinian Code, form the foundation of civil law systems used in most of the world, except for common-law countries like England and the United States. Roman architectural innovations including the arch, vault, concrete, and aqueduct enabled monumental construction and remained the template for Western architecture for centuries.

Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire under Constantine in three hundred thirteen CE. Rome remains the seat of the Catholic Church and the Vatican City, the world's smallest sovereign state. The city's enduring influence stems not merely from its ancient power but from the way its institutions shaped subsequent civilizations.

Today Rome stands as a repository of imperial ambition and cultural refinement, a place where the ancient world still speaks through its monuments and institutions. The Aeneid, Virgil's epic poem celebrating Rome's legendary founding and destiny, captures the city's significance in Western imagination. Rome's transformation from a settlement on the Tiber to the eternal city at the heart of Western civilization remains one of history's most remarkable stories.
